questions.question: 1. Consider the array: A = [9, 100, -1, 4, 8, 6, 9]. How many rounds of splitting (dividing) and how many total split operations are needed to break the array down for merge sort? (A round means all splits at the same level; a split operation means each time an array is divided.)

explanations.a: Incorrect. The number of rounds is the number of times we split all current subarrays, and the number of splits is the total number of times we divide any array. This answer mixes up the values.
explanations.b: Correct. For 7 elements, merge sort needs 3 rounds of splitting (since 2^3 = 8 > 7), and a total of 6 split operations to break the array down to single elements.
explanations.c: Incorrect. This answer reverses the meaning of rounds and splits.
explanations.d: Incorrect. This answer reverses the meaning of rounds and splits.

questions.question: 2. During which step of merge sort does the actual sorting happen?

explanations.a: Incorrect. Splitting just breaks the array into smaller pieces; no sorting happens here.
explanations.b: Incorrect. There is no separate sorting step in merge sort.
explanations.c: Correct. Sorting happens when merging the subarrays back together.

questions.question: 3. Which of the following best describes how the merge step works in merge sort (for ascending order)?

answers.a: We just join the subarrays one after the other.
answers.b: We compare the first elements of each subarray, add the smaller one to the result, and repeat until all elements are merged.
answers.c: We alternate picking elements from each subarray regardless of value.

explanations.a: Incorrect. We cannot just join the subarrays; we must compare values to keep the result sorted.
explanations.b: Correct. We always compare the smallest remaining elements and add the smaller one to the merged array.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Alternating elements does not guarantee a sorted result.
